title: OCIH 13 — Test
src: Anatomy & Functions of the Maxillary Sinus

mcqs.q: The paranasal sinuses all drain into the:
opts: Middle meatus of the lateral nasal wall
mcqs.explain: The paranasal air sinuses communicate and open into the lateral wall of the nasal cavity, draining into the middle meatus.

mcqs.q: Which paranasal sinus is the FIRST to develop?
mcqs.explain: The maxillary sinus is the first to develop, beginning in the 2nd gestational month as an invagination of the nasal cavity into the maxilla.

mcqs.q: The maxillary sinus is also known as the:
mcqs.explain: The maxillary sinus, which lies in the maxillary bone under the eyes, is known as the antrum of Highmore.

mcqs.q: The maxillary sinus is which shape, and how does it compare in size?
opts: Pyramidal, and it is the largest sinus
mcqs.explain: It is a pyramidal (tetrahedral) cavity of ~15 mL — the largest of the paranasal sinuses.

mcqs.q: The BASE of the pyramidal maxillary sinus (its medial wall) is formed by the:
opts: Lateral wall of the nasal cavity
mcqs.explain: The base of the pyramid (medial wall) is the lateral wall of the nasal cavity; the apex extends into the zygomatic process.

mcqs.q: The ROOF of the maxillary sinus is formed by the:
mcqs.explain: The roof is the floor of the orbit; it is the thinnest wall and the infraorbital canal runs along it.

mcqs.q: The FLOOR of the maxillary sinus is close to the:
opts: Apices of the upper molars and premolars
mcqs.explain: The floor is the alveolar process, often close to the apices of the upper molars and premolars — important in dental practice.

mcqs.q: The infraorbital canal (carrying the infraorbital nerve/vessels) runs in which wall?
mcqs.explain: The roof (thinnest wall) carries the infraorbital canal; tumours here can erode it and cause neurological symptoms.

mcqs.q: The posterior wall of the maxillary sinus contains the:
opts: Posterosuperior alveolar canal (PSA nerves to the molars)
mcqs.explain: The posterior (infratemporal) wall contains the posterosuperior alveolar canal; acute sinusitis can therefore cause pain in posterior maxillary teeth.

mcqs.q: The growth of the maxillary sinus is biphasic, occurring at ages:
mcqs.explain: Maxillary sinus growth is biphasic (0–3 and 7–12 years); pneumatization spreads inferiorly as permanent teeth erupt.

mcqs.q: The main blood supply to the maxillary sinus is from branches of the:
mcqs.explain: Branches of the maxillary artery (infraorbital, greater palatine, anterior and posterosuperior alveolar) supply the sinus.

mcqs.q: Venous drainage of the maxillary sinus is into the facial vein and the pterygoid plexus — clinically important because infection can spread to the:
mcqs.explain: The pterygoid plexus connects to the cavernous sinus, so sinus/facial infections can spread there — a dangerous pathway.

mcqs.q: Lymphatic drainage of the anterior sinus and floor is mainly to the:
mcqs.explain: The anterior part and floor drain to submandibular nodes; the posterior part drains to deep cervical nodes.

mcqs.q: Which is a function of the paranasal sinuses?
opts: Warming/humidifying air, increasing voice resonance and lightening the skull
mcqs.explain: Functions include warming/humidifying inhaled air, ventilation, aiding olfaction, increasing voice resonance, decreasing skull weight, shock absorption and immune defence.

mcqs.q: Why is the maxillary sinus important when extracting upper posterior teeth?
opts: Their roots lie close to the sinus floor, so an oroantral communication may occur
The roots are inside the orbit
The teeth contain the nerve supply
mcqs.explain: The roots of upper posterior teeth are very close to the sinus floor, so extraction can perforate it, causing an oroantral communication/fistula and chronic sinusitis.

mcqs.q: When the sinus floor is too low to place an implant, the procedure performed is a:
mcqs.explain: A sinus lift procedure augments the available bone volume when the maxillary sinus floor is too low for implant placement.

mcqs.q: On a radiograph, the maxillary antrum appears as:
opts: A radiolucent cavity with corticated radiopaque walls
mcqs.explain: The antrum appears as a radiolucent cavity with well-defined, dense, corticated radiopaque margins (walls).

mcqs.q: The GOLD STANDARD radiographic view for detecting fluid levels in maxillary sinusitis is the:
mcqs.explain: The Water's (occipitomental/paranasal sinus) view is the gold standard for assessing fluid levels in the maxillary sinus.

mcqs.q: Which sinuses lie within the labyrinth of the ethmoid bone (between nasal cavity and orbit)?
mcqs.explain: The ethmoidal sinuses are numerous intercommunicating spaces (6–12 per side) within the ethmoid labyrinth, between the nasal cavity and orbit.

mcqs.q: The anterior (facial) wall of the maxillary sinus is clinically important because:
opts: It is close to upper premolar/molar roots, allowing dental infection to spread into the sinus
mcqs.explain: The anterior wall is close to the roots of the upper premolars/molars, so dental infections can spread into the sinus and extractions may cause oroantral communication.

mcqs.q: On a periapical radiograph, the maxillary sinus floor in adults extends from:
opts: The distal aspect of the canine to the posterior wall above the tuberosity
The central incisor to the canine only
mcqs.explain: On IOPAR the sinus floor appears as a thin radiopaque line extending from the distal aspect of the canine to the posterior wall above the tuberosity.

mcqs.q: An air sinus is defined as:
mcqs.explain: Air sinuses are air-filled cavities within bone; those around the nasal cavity are the paranasal air sinuses.

mcqs.q: Acute maxillary sinusitis can present with pain that mimics:
opts: Pain in multiple posterior maxillary teeth
mcqs.explain: Because the PSA nerves run in the posterior wall, acute sinusitis can cause pain in several posterior maxillary teeth.

mcqs.q: The apex of the pyramidal maxillary sinus extends into the:
mcqs.explain: The apex of the pyramid extends laterally into the zygomatic process of the maxilla.

saqs.q: Name the paranasal sinuses and where they drain.
saqs.a: Frontal, ethmoidal, sphenoidal and maxillary air sinuses — air-filled bony cavities that drain into the middle meatus of the lateral nasal wall.

saqs.q: Describe the structure and boundaries of the maxillary sinus.
saqs.a: Pyramidal, largest sinus (antrum of Highmore). Base = lateral nasal wall (medial wall); apex = zygomatic process; roof = orbital floor; floor = alveolar process (near molar/premolar apices).

saqs.q: Why is the roof and posterior wall of the maxillary sinus important?
saqs.a: Roof = thinnest, carries the infraorbital canal/nerve (tumours → neurological signs). Posterior wall = PSA canal/nerves to the molars (sinusitis → posterior tooth pain).

saqs.q: State the blood, venous and nerve supply of the maxillary sinus.
saqs.a: Blood: branches of the maxillary artery. Venous: facial vein & pterygoid plexus (→ cavernous sinus, dangerous). Nerve: infraorbital + superior alveolar (ASA/MSA/PSA).

saqs.q: List the functions of the paranasal sinuses.
saqs.a: Warm & humidify air, act as an air reservoir/ventilation, aid olfaction, increase voice resonance, decrease skull weight, shock absorption and immune defence.

saqs.q: Explain the dental importance of the maxillary sinus.
saqs.a: Upper posterior tooth roots lie close to the floor — extraction risks oroantral communication/fistula → chronic sinusitis; a sinus lift augments bone when the floor is too low for an implant.

saqs.q: Describe the radiographic appearance and views for the maxillary sinus.
saqs.a: A radiolucent cavity with corticated radiopaque walls. Views: IOPAR, occlusal, OPG, and the Water's (occipitomental) view — gold standard for fluid levels; CT/MRI for detail.
